EXTENSIVE DAMAGE TO PROPERTY.
DUNGOG, Monday, 10:30 a.m.
Heavy rain commenced late on Saturday night and
continued to fall in torrents throughout Sunday till
late at night. It was the heaviest and biggest fall
ever experienced in this district. The local weather
gauge records over 854 points. The river and creeks
are flooded, and overflowed their banks. Farms have
been inundated, and great damage has been done to
all the crops.
The ground had just been ploughed for maize
planting. The heavy rains have completely washed
the top soil away. Several head of cattle have been
drowned, fences have been swept away, and gravel
off the roads washed out. A number of culverts
have been damaged.
Several houses in the town are almost flooded, and
the occupants are preparing to leave.
The mail coach between here and Maitland was
delayed several hours owing to the damage done to
the culverts.
The rain is still falling, and there is no sign of it
abating.
At Clarence Town over 9 inches have been recorded. The flood is several feet over the wharf.
Only meagre particulars are obtainable.
MORPETH, Monday.
The rainfall here up to 9 o'clock this morning is
616 points. The Hunter and Paterson rivers are
bankers. Narrowgut and a large portion of Phoenix
Park are under water.
The potato crop will be ruined.

A GOLD-BEARING REEF.
DISCOVERED AT EUCHAREENA.
Mr. J. B. Jaquet, Acting Chief Inspector of
Mines, has furnished the Under-Secretary of
that department, Mr. Pittman, with a report
concerning the discovery of a payable gold reef
upon the property of Mr. J. Dalton, about
eight miles from Euchareena. According to Mr.
Jaquet the reef occurs upon the rocky slope of
a low hill, and the outcrop is marked by a
permanent "blow" of white quartz. It must
have frequently attracted attention, but it is
only recently that the prospectors, Messrs.
Longmore and Woollard, demonstrated that it
was gold-bearing. "The reef," observes Mr.
Jaquet In his report, "would seem to consist of
elongated quartz cubes, which run parallel and
overlap one another, rather than a solid lode.
In places it includes breaks or intervals of
country rock, intersected by quartz leaders.
Gold has been proved to occur for a distance of
over 500ft along the outcrop. It would seem to
be mostly confined to the face or the hanging
wall, the roof ranging from a few inches to
18in. in width. About 60ft south of the shaft
the quartz is studded with particles of gold
which are visible to the naked eye. A parcel of
rich ore may be raised from near the surface at
this point. The shaft has been sunk to a
depth of 50ft with the aid of a grant from the
prospecting vote. Nothing further than this
has been done to prove the extent of the payable ore. The ground has been pegged out for
nearly a mile on each side of the prospectors'
claim." Euchareena is on the Great Western
railway line, about 20 miles beyond Orange.

KURRI KURRI LABOUR TROUBLES.
KURRI KURRI, Sunday.
The Hebburn miners, who are out on strike,
though they deprecate the use of such a
term, are using stringent measures to enforce
attendance of all members at the weekly
meetings. Hopes are entertained that a
settlement will be arrived at, in view of the
mine being taken on tribute by Messrs. Ralph
Turnbull and H. Savage, who have offered the
following terms to the men: - 10s 6d per day
for shooters down, with powder supplied free
of charge, and a bonus of 2 ¼d per ton to each
shooter for every ton over 56; fillers to receive
8d per ton; all the arrangements made
between the men and the company previous
to the trouble regarding deficient work to be
binding on the tributers. The men do not
approve of the terms offered by the tributers,
but the whole of the position is under consideration.
The Hebburn colliery horses were brought
from the company's paddock to Hebburn today.
The management of the Pelaw-Main Colliery
have declined to consider the proposals made
by the employees for increased pay in certain
portions of the mine, alleged to be very wet.
The matter will be referred to the district
board.

SYDNEY QUARTER SESSIONS.
(Before Judge Backhouse and juries.)
Mr Herbert Harris prosecuted for the
Crown.
ALLEGED THEFT.
Alfred Clark a kitchenman was charged
with stealing a quantity of clothing, a fish
fork and a saucepan, the property of Agnes
Ida Smith He was further charged with
having the property mentioned in his possession, well knowing it to have been stolen.
The evidence showed that the accused was
employed by the prosecutrix, who keeps a
boarding-house in Macleay-street. On December 22 he left his place and that night he
was arrested by Senior Constable Lonsdale
and taken to where he was lodging. On the
police wanting to search his room the accused resisted their efforts and violently
assaulted Constable Blair, for which he was
sentenced to six months' hard labour. Owing to his resistance the police were unable
to search the room, but the following morning they found the property mentioned in the
charge there.
The defence was a denial of any knowledge
of the stolen property, which the accused asserted had been placed in his room to secure
his conviction.
The jury returned a verdict of not guilty
on both counts, and the accused was discharged.
RECEIVING STOLEN PROPERTY.
Robert John Carmichael pleaded guilty to a
charge of receiving a coat, a pair of trousers, a vest, and a brooch, the property of
George Sewell, well knowing the same to have
been stolen. He also pleaded guilty to a
similar charge in connection with a quantity
of clothing and cutlery, the property of Henry
M'Credie.
The accused, who was defended by Mr. E. R.
Abigail, was remanded for sentence.
ALLEGED FALSE PRETENCES.
Robert Millett and Mary Edith Millett, his
wife pleaded not guilty to a charge of false
pretences. The indictment stated that on
October 9, 1906 the accused falsely pretended
to Hymen Lobel Friedman that Mary Edith
Millett had entered into a contract with
Henry Benjamin Pollard for the sale of certain land to him for £2500, and that the sum
of £1500 had been lodged in cash as a deposit in part payment by Pollard with George
Moffat Robinson, a conveyancer and that Pollard was a purchaser with money at his disposal to complete the purchase and did then
falsely promise Friedman that Pollard would
pay the balance of the purchase money and
by means of which promise the accused obtained from Friedman £50, with intent to do
fraud.
There were two other counts in which the
accused were charged with obtaining by similar representations from Friedman the sum
of £100 on October 12, and £200 on October 22.
Mr. J. C. Gannon instructed by Mr. W. E.
Hawkins appeared for the accused.
His Honor directed the jury to return a
verdict of not guilty against the female accused and she was discharged. The male accused was also found not guilty and acquitted.
SENTENCES
The following sentences were passed: - William Morris breaking and entering two years'
hard labour, Charles Campbell, false presences, one year and a day; Robert Anderson
indecent assault, three years' penal servitude.

IN DIVORCE.
(Before Mr. Justice Owen.)
ROBINSON v ROBINSON.
The petitioner, Annie Montague Robinson
(formerly Mathews), sued for a decree for
judicial separation from Hubert William
Robinson, on the ground of alleged cruelty.
The parties were married in 1903, according to
the rites of the Presbyterian Church, at Redfern. Mr. Toose (instructed by Mr. J. W.
Abigail) appeared for the petitioner, and Mr.
Reimer (instructed by Mr. E. R. Abigail) for
the respondent, who denied his wife's allegations. A decree nisi was granted, returnable
in six months.
GOLDSTEIN v GOLDSTEIN.
A decree nisi, returnable in six months, was
granted in a suit by Monte Goldstein for
divorce, from Lila May Goldstein (formerly
Donohoe), on the ground of alleged adultery
with one Lionel Lunn, who was joined as co-respondent. The petitioner and respondent
were married at the District Registry, St.
Leonards. In 1915. Mr. Toose (instructed by
Mr. W. H. Drew) appeared for the petitioner.
ALEXANDER v ALEXANDER.
In this suit, Mary Alice Alexander (formerly
Donovan) petitioned for a divorce from
Reginald Crawford Alexander, on the ground
of desertion. The parties were married at
St. Patrick's Church, Fortitude Valley, Brisbane, in 1919. Mr. N. Cherry Willis represented the petitioner, who was granted a
decree nisi, to be moved absolute in six
months.
BALFOUR v BALFOUR.
An order for restitution of conjugal rights
was made in the suit of Adelaide Louisa Balfour (formerly Pratten) against Charles Balfour, the couple having been married in 1912,
at St Andrew's Church. Walkerville (S.A.),
Mr. Collins (instructed by Messrs. Beehag
and Simpson, Sydney agents for Mr. Beehag,
of Rockdale) appeared for the petitioner.
NEAL v NEAL.
A suit, raising the issue of desertion, was
instituted by Charles Frederick Neal against
Edith Ella Neal (formerly Harigold), the parties having been married at Sydney In 1905,
according to the rites of the Whitefield Congregational Church. Mr. James Young (instructed by Mr. R. Harris) appeared for petitioner The petition was dismissed on account of unreasonable delay in proceeding
with the suit.
DEAN v DEAN.
In this suit, John Henry Dean petitioned for
a divorce from Beatrice Dean (formerly Gordon), alleging adultery with one William Wall,
who was joined as co-respondent. The couple
were married at the District Registry, Wilton
(Eng.), in 1919. Mr. Collins (instructed by
Messrs. Beehag and Simpson, Sydney agents
for Mr. F. W. Beehag, of Rockdale) appeared
for the petitioner. A decree nisi was granted,
returnable in six months.
AHEARN v AHEARN.
The petitioner in this case, Amy May Ahearn
(formerly Smith), sued for a dissolution of
her marriage with Leopold Ahearn, alleging
adultery with a woman named Alice Margaret Durrance, also desertion. The parties
were married in 1911 at Sydney, according to
the rites of the Church of England. Mr.
Small (instructed by Mr. P. J. Clines) appeared
for the petitioner, who was granted a decree
nisi returnable in six months.
MORETON v MORETON.
Ada Burdett Moreton (formerly Finney)
petitioned for a divorce from Arthur Preston
Moreton, alleging desertion by reason of noncompliance with an order of the Court for the
restitution of conjugal rights. The parties
were married at St. Michael's Church, Darlinghurst, in 1915. Mr. Moors (instructed by Mr.
J. McLeod) appeared for the petitioner, who
was granted a decree, returnable in six
months.
KENNEDY v KENNEDY.
On the ground of desertion, Frederick
Gilbert Kennedy sued for a divorce from
Annie Emil Kennedy (formerly Benschell)
to whom he was married in 1897 according to
the rites of the Church of England. Mr.
Lionel Dare (instructed by Mr. Reginald
Thornton), appeared for the petitioner. A
decree nisi was granted, returnable in six
months.
FRERE v FRERE.
A decree for the restitution of conjugal
rights was granted in the suit of Victor
Emanuel Frere against his wife, Amy Carrie
Frere (formerly Lawrence), to whom he was
married in 1924 at Balmain, according to the
rites of the Church of England. Mr. Lionel
Dare (instructed by Mr. R. Thornton) appeared for the petitioner.
HUMBY v HUMBY.
Euphemia Catherine Humby (formerly Conway), the petitioner in this suit, sued for a
divorce from William Henry Humby on the
ground of desertion. The parties were married at St. Stephen's, Penrith, In 1911. Mr.
Collins (Instructed by Messrs. A. E. What-more, G. C. M. Gee, and Co.) appeared for the
petitioner, who was granted a decree, to be
moved absolute in six months.
JACKSON v JACKSON.
A decree nisi returnable in six months was
granted in a suit in which Stuart Francis
Jackson petitioned for a divorce from Agnes
Winnifred Jackson (formerly Brindley), alleging adultery with one, Sidney Arthur Perry,
who was joined as co-respondent. Petitioner
and respondent were married in 1911 at Sydney according to the rites of the Church of
England. Mr. Collins (Instructed by Mr.
Stephen Ahern) appeared for the petitioner.
WHEELER V WHEELER.
Horace Wheeler petitioned for a divorce
from Ruby May Wheeler (formerly Fisher),
alleging adultery with one David Smith, who
was joined as co-respondent. Petitioner and
respondent were married in 1915, according
to the rites of the Church of England. Mr.
Rowley (Messrs. Rowley, Roseby, and Co,)
appeared for the petitioner; who was granted
a decree, returnable in six months.

DEATH OF MRS. D. C.
McLACHLAN.
Memories of the days when Darlinghurst
and Paddington were divided by Boundary
Creek, and when most of the populous area
between William-street and the harbour was
held in Government grants, are recalled by
the death on Saturday of Mrs. Emily M.
McLachlan, wife of Mr. Duncan Clark
McLachlan, C.M.G., I.S.O., of Mosman.
Mrs. McLachlan was in her 81st year. She
was a daughter of the late Mr. Obed West,
who inherited Barcom Glen Estate, upon
which much of Darlinghurst and Rushcutter
Bay is built, from his father. The latter
received the estate as a Government grant,
leaving it to his son In 1810, it was on
portion of the property, which extended to
the water at Rushcutter Bay, that Mrs.
McLachlan was born. The estate still remains in the West family, of whom two sisters
and one brother survive, though most of it
has been leased. The Rushcutter Bay portion was resumed by the Government some
years ago.
Mr. McLachlan, who survives his wife, was
formerly Under-Secretary for Mines and Agriculture in New South Wales. After Federation he became the first Commonwealth Public Service Commissioner. He retired from
that position in 1916, when he left Melbourne
to make his home in Mosman. For some years,
too, he was chairman of directors of the
Civil Service Stores In Sydney.
Three sons and three daughters also survive. They are Misses Ethel and Thirza
McLachlan and Mrs. H. L. Butler, Messrs.
A. L. and S. C. McLachlan, of Sydney, and
R. O. McLachlan, of Stockinbingal.
The funeral took place yesterday afternoon
at St. Jude's Cemetery, Randwick. The principal mourners were Mr. D. C. McLachlan and
the three sons. Mr. A. O. West (brother),
Mr H. L. Butler (son-in-law), and Messrs.
E. Marriott, H. Ellis. A. Hudson, B. McLachlan, and H. West (nephews). Others present
were Messrs. E. C. Cragen (formerly Commonwealth Public Service Inspector for New
South Wales), Duncan (representing the Commonwealth Public Service), C. W. Kelety
(manager) and T. Garratt (director) of the
Civil Service Stores, and F. A. Coghlan (formerly Auditor-General).

VISIT OF AMERICAN WRITERS.
TO THE EDITOR OF THE HERALD.
Sir,—I wish to support the remarks of Mr.
Charles Lloyd Jones in this morning's issue.
As one who has played some little part in
advertising Australia abroad, and in attracting
tourists to the country, I cordially approve
of the methods of the Australian National
Travel Association, and I consider that the
gentlemen who control that organisation, and
who give their services to the country voluntarily have done work of extraordinary value
to Australia. But nothing they have done up
to date is of more value than this latest move
of securing a visit from some of America's
most noted publicists. No one could estimate
the effect of this visit, and it would be impossible to calculate its value in money. It
is easy enough to criticise, and there is far
too much carping criticism here of any effort
by public men. But this particular move is
beyond criticism, and I am amazed that anyone could have found fault with it.
I am, etc.,
PERCY HUNTER.
Sydney, Jan. 16.

Earlier Report to

OUR WAR CORRESPONDENT,
JACK PERCIVAL
MANILA, Feb 25.—Among the
prisoners rescued at Los Banos
concentration camp was W. H.
Donald, an Australian who was
confidential adviser to Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek, and his
secretary, Miss Ainsie Lee.
When the prison camp at Santo
Tomas was captured from the
Japanese a story was current that
Donald was among the prisoners
rescued here. At that time I wrote
a report stating that Donald had spent
about three years in Santo Tomas
working as a bookbinder. This was
true, but Donald had transferred to
Los Banos a few months before the
Americans reached Manila.
The reason for this story about his
imprisonment in Santo Tomas was to
make the Japanese believe that he was
out of their clutches.

A DISCOVERY.
THE BODY OF DE SOTO FOUND WHERE IT
WAS BURIED CENTURIES AGO.
[From the New Orleans National Republican.]
Our readers may remember that about
eighteen months ago an article appeared
in some of our most reliable papers making known some important facts. It stated
that Capt. Blank, an old and well-known
explorer of our great river and its numerous tributaries, together with the many bay-ous which traverse and intersect our state,
had made some interesting discoveries in
regard to the small islands dotted about
here and there in the river and shallow
lakes of Southern Louisiana.
Among the most remarkable of these
islands noted and explored by Capt. Blank,
are two not very remote from this city,
and well-known to all steamboatmen on
the river. It seems that Captn. Blank, although so very enterprising and energetic,
is a man quite advanced in years, being
now in his sixty-ninth year. Having
spent his life on the river since childhood,
he remembered that about forty years
ago a fine vessel, hailing from Bordeaux,
and laden with the best French wines,
champagnes, cordials, etc., were sunk at
or near the spot where one of these islands, which had then no existence, now
stands. This vessel with her cargo was
owned by parties in France, but was consigned to the care of a well-known house
in New Orleans, which exists still.
Capt. Blank conceived the idea that this
valuable cargo might be rescued from its
watery bed by means of diving bells, and
consequently he employed several experienced divers to examine the wreck and report whether it was possible to reach the
hull of this long sunken vessel.
The divers made a thorough examination and reported the plan practicable but
very expensive. Capt. Blank applied to
the house to whom the vessel had originally been consigned and showed the report of the divers. This enterprising
house, knowing that a vast fortune would
reward them if the undertaking was successful, willingly assisted the captain with
men and means to work out his apparently
wild speculation; and the result has
proved that wonders will never cease; for
at last, after more than one year from the
time the enterprise was begun, Capt. Blank
has really succeeded in raising at least
one-half of the valuable cargo, which has
been sweetening and mellowing beneath
the father of waters for nearly a half cen-During his researches among the several
bayous of southern Louisiana, he discovered an island about five miles below
what is known as the "Old Forts", and in
the bed of what is termed by steamboat-men "Old River." This old river was
once the natural bed of the Mississippi ;
but it cut through a narrow neck of land,
and formed another outlet. In this
stream Captain Blank noticed an island,
which he felt convinced was formed over
some wreck. One day while wandering
over it, he discovered beneath the marshy
grass something that looked like the bow
of a boat. He carefully cut away the
long tough grass, and we may judge his
surprise when he actually made out the
bow of a boat, apparently in excellent
preservation. It was strongly built and
copper bound, and was an ancient-looking
craft. It seemed to rest upon its stern,
which was entirely covered by the soil,
which had accumulated over it, while the
roots of an immense tree beneath the bow
were lifting it from its bed.
Capt. Blank determined, a few months
since, to excavate this ancient craft, or at
least what was left of it. The work progressed rapidly with the aid of a powerful dredging machine, and after three
months hard work the Captain had the
happiness of reaching the hatchway of the
half-rotten vessel, but day by day passed
and nothing was brought to light of any
real value. A few rusted swords, scab-bards pieces of rusty armor were brought
up, which being examined by Capt. Blank,
proved the vessel to have been of Spanish
build. The workmen were disgusted
with their useless labor, and had determined to give up their vain enterprise,
when lo! they came upon something
which they firmly believed to be a box of
gold. Their cupidity and curiosity being
excited, they worked hard to raise it from
its bed of compact mud. Their disgust,
however, was great when the object
brought up proved to be a blacksmith's
anvil, with Spanish characters wrought
upon it.
Capt. Blank, who watched the proceedings with an eager eye, besought the men
to continue a few days longer, when at
last they came to something which, this
time, they felt convinced, was a box of
Mexic gold - perhaps hidden there by
Capt. Kidd himself. But we may imagine
the awe and astonishment of the Captain
and the workmen when the object was
raised and cleared of its mud, and laid
before them. It was evidently a human
body, completely and perfectly wrapped
in lead - air and water-tight. Around the
lead covering was firmly welded a broad
copper band with its Spanish inscription,
rudely wrought upon it, which being
cleared of its rust and mud, revealed the
following words :
Aqui yacen los restos de
Hernando De Soto,
Que fallecio el dia
15 de Mayo, de 1542, A. D.,
de edad de cuarenta y cuatro anos y siete
messes.
Each man uncovered his head and remained standing in solemn awe as the
body was examined. Capt. Blank felt
convinced that it was the body of the
great Spaniard, which as every school
child knows, was buried in his boat, and
sunk at midnight in the bosom of the
great Mississippi, to keep the knowledge
of his death from the Indians, and in all
probability the anvil was placed in the
boat to assist it in settling steadily down.
The body of De Soto was brought to the
city yesterday, and is now lying in the
Mayor's parlor at the City Hall. To-mor-
row we learn it will be taken to the
School of Medicine, on Baronne street,
when its leaden wrapping will be removed,
and in all probability the remains of DeSoto will be laid bare to the reverential
eyes of those who live along the banks of
the mighty Mississippi, whose waters have
at length yielded up the body of its great
discoverer.

Mr. P. C. Jones is here. He promised to borrow sufficient money,
West of the Rockey Mountains to
refund the National Loan of Hawaii. But he didn't.
He crossed the Rockey Mountains
and met his friends the Boston
deacons, he saw Gorham Gilman
the "Star of Bethlehem," and he
travelled to New York. He had
with him Mr. Rithet, an Englishman
from Canada, who, according to Mr.
Jones is an export borrower.
Alas! Jones and Rithet travelled
and trotted in the East, but not a
bean could the great financiers raise
from the "mean" capitalists, East of
the Rockey Mountains. Jones says,
it was because he had no papers
from Damon, showing his authority
to borrow money. Damon emits
one of his finest smiles and says,
that Jones is welcome to go right
ahead, and do all the refunding he
can. His Excellency is even willing
to see our heavy-weight ex-Minister
of Finance, go into the spool and
shuttle business again and get
another financial lesson.
Joking apart, let us ask any fair-minded man how this Government
can expect to borrow money, and
why any sane person in America or
Europe should be found willing to
loan money to Mr. Jones or any
other agent of Dole's oligarchy.
Hawaii is now in the throes of a
revolution. The Republic is tottering towards its final resting place,
and to the honor of the men at its
head, be it said that they are only
too willing to step down and out
and make room for a Government,
which will be acceptable to the people, and at the same time have the
welfare of all classes as their ultimate object.
The Hawaiian Republic cannot
exist in its present form. We regret
to a certain extent that the fate of
downfall stares our Administration
in the face. The members of Mr.
Dole's funny little Republic are
good and true men in most points.
They have not, however, got the
people back of them and what is a
Government against the people?
The situation to-day shows that an
immense majority is opposed to the
present Government. Their friends
of old have turned against the
"missionaries" to a man. The faithful Portuguese colony are tired of
broken promises and stand united
against Mr. Dole. The Catholics of
all nationalities have felt the influence of our local A. P. A. headed by
Chief Justice Judd and irrespective
of political creeds they stand
ready to down the Protestant Government which dares to bring religion into politics. The army is disgruntled and the case now to be
tried before a military court will
probably lead to an open rupture.
The President and his Ministers are
seeking the friendship of the Hawaiians but all they got is the
"marble" heart. The Hawaiian can
stomach everything from gin and
poi to a kick. He cannot swallow
Mr. Dole and the prospects of losing
the independence of his country.
Under these circumstances can
any reasonable man expect that an
American syndicate will come to
the front and open their coffers for
the benefit of the Bunker Hill hero
and pour their coin into Mr.
Jones' ample lap?
It will be well for our financial
friends, at the west or east of the
Rocky Mountains to go slow and
find out how the land of Hawaii lies,
tone of the bland Mr. P. C. Jones.
Hawaiian bonds may be good even
if handled by Mr. Jones, and issued
at 4 percent interest. At the same
time inventors should get on to
facts and that is what Mr. Jones
does not give them.
The Jones official financiering and
his refunding business are all talk.
And what a lot of gas there is in our
copious friend. Let Hawaii get on
a sound basis with a stable Government and an administration entitled to the respect of the world
and her credit will be all right and
the special services of Mr. Jones
unnecessary. Until then, our fair
islands will remain in a constant
state of bankruptcy and the people
will be in the Consomme which Mr.
Jones desires to skim.

Honolulu, July 21, 1896.
The immense fortunes that
are now being invested in bicycle manufacturing in nearly all
countries of the world, even including modernized little Japan,
are thrilling to read of.
These little horse-destroying
conveniences are now being
manufactured by the millions
instead of by the few hundreds
of ten or fifteen years ago, and
it is estimated by a cyclist
authority that they are at least
7000 different patents and designs in connection with them.
But we note, in an English
exchange, the curious fact that
the palaces and parks of the
die-hard aristocracy are gradually succumbing to the inevitable
and passing into the hands of
the cyclist autocrats. The item
informs us that Trafford Park
Sir H. de Trafford's seat near
Manchester, has been purchased
for £360,000, ($1,800,000) by
the syndicate which recently acquired the Dunlop Tyre and
Singer Co. It is proposed to
make the estate the seat of the
cycle and rubber trade.
Now, we have made such a
success of our different brands
of wheels that our fame has
gone abroad. We have our own
predilictions in favor of a certain make, but, when, unsolicited, we received a consignment
of a popularly favorite brand
without a flaw, perfection itself
in strength, beauty and shape
and manufactured by a worldwide known firm, we could not
be discourteous enough to return
them, without endeavoring to
put them on the market. The
fact is we have had six of those
celebrated Zimmerman champion wheels for gentlemen sent
to us, and we invite cyclists to
call and inspect them and to use
their own judgment as to
whether they want them or not.
As they have been sent to us
on consignment, we prefer to
sell them and close the consignment, instead of returning them.
We therefore offer them at $75
each instead of at the regular
price of $100. We admit that
they are beauties and we don't
think they will be on our hands
for many days, but as we have
only half a dozen on hand, the
first applicant will have his
pick. They are first-class high
grade machines and very tempting to experts.

Double Government in the
Old Blue
Grass State,
and Serious

Their New Commander — Taylor's

FRANKFORT, Ky., Jan. 31. - Never
was there a more complicated political situation than that which tonight confronts the politicians of
Kentucky, and never was there one
of which it seemed so difficult to form an
accurate guess at the outcome.
William Goebel, who was shot down by
an assassin yesterday, received the oath
of office as Governor of Kentucky tonight. What the legislators were kept
from doing publicly they accomplished by
stealth.
All day through the streets of Frankfort
soldiers marched and countermarched.
Drills in the street were frequently held,
in order that the men might be warmed
by exercise after they had remained in the
biting wind.
Around the Penitentiary was a line of
troops, in front of the opera-house was a
guard, three companies stood at rest in
the open space in front of the Capitol
Hotel, sentries patrolled every side of the
building in which ex-Governor Bradley
resides and a detachment of infantry held
the courthouse against the possible coming of the members of the Legislature
with the intention of declaring that not
the living William S. Taylor, but the
dying William Goebel, was the lawful
head and executive of the commonwealth
of Kentucky.
The Republicans laid their plans well
and secretly. They carried them through
vigorously. The proclamation declaring that a state of insurrection
existed in the State and warrants for
the arrest of every Democratic member of the Legislature were prepared last
night. It was the intention of Governor
Taylor and his advisers that no meeting
of the Legislature should be held to-day
even though it proved necessary to arrest
and detain in custody all those who persisted in holding meetings. Once adopted
the policy was carried out to the letter.
Compelled to retire from the Capitol
building they went to the opera-house.
Held back from the opera-house they
went to the courthouse; prevented from
entering the courthouse they went to the
Capitol Hotel, only to be told that any
meeting they might attempt to hold in
that building would be suppressed, all
found taking part in it would be arrested
and the hotel itself seized by the soldiers.

had no chance to win and they gave it
up. Later in the day officers entered the
hotel and told the Democrats that no conferences should be held and they attempted to hold none.
Governor Taylor and his attorneys remained all night in the State House.
Threats had been made against all of
them, and it was thought the wisest thing
for them was to remain where they were
until the excitement had in some degree
abated.
This morning not a member of the Legislature knew whether or not the body
would be permitted to meet in the Capitol
building. They knew that soldiers were
guarding every gate and that nobody
would be allowed to enter without a pass.
They decided, however, to meet at the
Capitol Hotel and march in a body to the
Capitol. Clerk Edward Lee of the House,
with Representatives Kilday and Lewis,

squad. As soon as the members of the
Legislature were identified they were admitted and allowed to pass into the Capitol building. Not a soldier was in sight
on the outside of the building, but once
the door was opened it looked like war.

000 tons of copper annually, which is
used mainly in the construction of
those copper and brass cooking pots
and other utensils used there from
time immemorial. An attempt is now
being made to replace these metals by
aluminum, the initiative in the matter
being due to Mr. A. Chatterton, professor of engineering at the Madras
University, says London Engineering,
Professor Chatterton, on his return to
India last November, took with him a
small quantity of aluminum and commenced experiments with it at the
metal working classes of the School of
Arts, Madras, of which he was the director. A little later a small factory
was equipped and the products were
so favorably received that the output
in the course of five months amounted
to considerably over a ton per month.
This result is somewhat surprising, in
view of the intense conservatism of the
Indian people. Nevertheless, this latter feeling, though it has not resulted
very actively a change of material, is
still strongly displayed, in so far as
the forms and finish of these cooking
vessels are concerned. The shapes of
the new vessel must, to be acceptable,
be exactly the same as the old; and the
matter is somewhat complicated, as
these traditional pots differ in every
district. Further, the vessel must be
all hand-made, as drawn or spun work
is disliked, in spite of its greater cheapness. An attempt to meet the native
wishes in this matter while at the same
time reducing the cost of the utensils,
is now being made. A drawing press is
used to accomplish the initial stages
of the work, which is then finished by
hand. Some of the Indian workmen
are said to be now very skillful in the
use of the new material, and efforts are
being made to establish similar factories elsewhere. The aluminum used
has, up to the present time, been obtained from the British Aluminium
company. - Western Mining World.

number of women engaged in the work,

Hull reports that 50,000$ has been

The mines adjoin those of the United
Verde and while they are but partially
developed at present it is announced
that the big ore bodies of the latter
properties are known to extend into
the Extension company's claims.

SENATE TO ACT
ON EXTENSION OF
D. C. RENT ACT
Amendment to Statute Would
Repay Back Rent to Tenants
Under Favorable Decisions.
Senator Ball today introduced his
resolution extending the Ball Rent
Commission act for a seven-month
period in the Senate.
The resolution provides that the
rent law shall be continued from
October 22 next until May 22, 1922.
It provides that the Rent Commissioners shall be paid a salary of
$5,000 a year and the secretary $3,000
a year. It also provides the commission with a counsel who shall
represent the commission in all litigation.
Garages, hotels, and other business
properties are exempted from the
terms of the resolution. Senator
Ball hopes that the resolution will
be passed without debate. There is
a considerable group in the Senate,
however, which will attempt to extend the Rent Commission act for
longer than the seven-month period
provided for in the resolution.
An important amendment to the
Rent Commission act was placed in
the resolution as presented to the Senate. It provides a method by which
tenants can recover back rent that is
owing them under decisions of the
Commission. Its text is as follows:
"That in all cases where the owner
has prior to April 18, 1921, collected
any excess rent or charge, he may return such excess to tenants direct, and
in default of his so doing upon application by the tenant to the Commission, a rule shall be issued against
such owner and served in the same
manner as other notices from the
Commission, requiring such owners to
refund such excess to the tenant within ten days from the service of such
rule, and in default of such refund
within the said ten days, the Commission shall proceed to recover double the amount of the excess with
costs and attorneys' fees as herein
provided."
The Senate District committee will
meet at 2 o'clock tomorrow afternoon
to take up street railway merger legislation.
